rationale: A wins because it knows where the factual floor is. Its strongest line, "the actual roles cut versus left unfilled — which Klarna currently won't disclose," protects the founder from the mistake B makes in "the Equivalent of 700 People Are Gone," which turns a workload equivalent into phantom humans. B has usable shapes, but its headlines keep spending facts it has not earned.
gaps_in_A: "When your BNPL dispute is decided by a chatbot" overstates the update. The facts say advocates raised concerns about AI handling disputes, not that the chatbot decides them.
"Klarna cut average chat resolution from 11 minutes to under 2 — here's how" needs the resolved-versus-escalated definition before it becomes more than Klarna's own efficiency stat.

"A profitable, IPO-bound Klarna leans on AI it won't fully explain" slightly blurs two different unknowns: AI methodology and cut-versus-unfilled headcount opacity. Both need proof before that headline is safe.
gaps_in_B: "But the Equivalent of 700 People Are Gone" is the big sin. The update says the assistant handled work equivalent to 700 full-time agents, not that 700 people disappeared.

"The Headcount It Cut Is the Margin It's Showing Investors" invents a financial causal chain. The facts say Klarna is profitable and headcount fell; they do not prove the headcount drop is the margin story.
"advocacy concerns surfacing now are likely to precede regulatory attention" adds a fake news peg and a speculative regulator arc. Nothing in the update says that.
"Before this, AI-in-customer-service claims were largely vendor-produced" is unsupported industry wallpaper. It sounds smart until a reporter asks, "according to whom?"
